newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Peters says time has come for pension savings.
newsitem.headline: NZ Peters says time has come for pension savings.

text.p: New Zealand's Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters said on Monday the time was right for the country's proposed Retirement Savings Scheme (RSS), which is to be considered in a September referendum.
Detailing the much-vaunted scheme for the first time, Peters told a news conference the plan's motivation was clear.
"There is nothing more powerful than an idea whose time has come," he told an audience that included representatives of the pension industry which is expected to manage contributed funds.
"(It) solves the problem of future affordability posed by the impending retirement of the baby boom generation," he said.
New Zealand's population, like those of many other developed nations, surged after the end of World War II and its rate of growth has since slowed.
This means that, almost a century after it launched a pioneering universal state pension scheme, New Zealand now believes it will struggle to support ever-higher payouts.

"Next century it will be harder to provide an adequate retirement income from taxation. As a greater percentage of the population retires the ratio of workers to retired people will grow smaller and smaller," Peters said.
The combination of a requirement for compulsory savings with proposed tax cuts is meant to make the introduction of RSS self-financing for the working public.
Its target is to ensure every person in employment has saved enough for an annuity equivalent to 33 percent of the average, ordinary time, after-tax wage.
"This income is tax-free and everyone will be receiving it for as long as they live," Peters said, adding that the income would be inflation-indexed to retain its purchasing power.

To address the fears of people established in employment, or nearing retirement, RSS is to be phased in over 40 years with only those born after April 1, 1973, having to contribute in full when it is envisaged to start up next July.

Peters declined to say how much state money would be involved in setting up the scheme and providing the many top-ups which he has said would be included to ensure the same level of minimum benefit is available to all.
This set of provisions, which Treasury calls its income guarantee, made RSS "fair to all New Zealanders", he said.
One example is a planned equalisation payment which would be given to women so that their annuity has the same value as men's without having to cost more in contributions.
"Because women on average live longer than men, the government will pay all women a top-up to purchase the standard annuity, which is more expensive for women than for men," Peters explained.
Peters was pressed by reporters on why the government has chosen not to guarantee savings put into privately-managed funds.
He argued that the risk would lie with industry players, who were required to have reinsurance, and also with the government which would pledge to top up any savings that fell short.
The initial reaction from pensions industry participants at the presentation was that the scheme outline was comprehensive.

Although a full public information campaign has been planned to start up at the end of this month, a pamphlet summarising the 86-page white paper is to be distributed to all households on Tuesday, Peters said.
